reading.rtitle: Very Good Is Not Good Enough: Passion in a Second Language
paras: Last month in São Paulo, a friend took me to a tiny record shop near Avenida Paulista. He is a die-hard fan of American soul, and he has been hooked on it since he was fifteen. In Portuguese, he talked about the records for an hour, and his enthusiasm was absolutely infectious. Then he turned to me and said, in English, 'This music is very good.' It was such a strange moment. The passion was all there, but the words were utterly flat.

It happens to almost everyone who speaks a second language. We learn very and good early, and we use them for everything. But English has two kinds of adjectives. Some, like good, loud or tired, can be stronger or weaker, so we say very good or extremely loud. Others, like brilliant, deafening or exhausted, are already extreme. Nothing can be a little bit brilliant, so we say absolutely brilliant or totally exhausted, never very brilliant. Really is the safe one: it works with both.

A week later, I watched a match in a bar in Liverpool with a man who lives and breathes his club. When they scored, the place went absolutely wild, and he told me that the atmosphere at the stadium is so electric that it gives him goosebumps every time. He did not use long words. He just chose the right ones. So the next time you talk about what you love, do not say it is very good. Say it is absolutely amazing, and then tell people why.
reading.source: Adapted from a column by Fiona Reid

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the column?
choices: Soul music and football are the two best ways for adults to learn English quickly, because both of them are full of very strong emotions.
People often sound flat when they talk about their passions in a second language, and the right adjective and intensifier can fix that.

items: The writer's friend has loved soul music since he was a teenager.
She says he has been hooked on it since he was fifteen.
In English, the friend described the records with strong, exciting words.
He only said 'very good', and his words were utterly flat.
According to the writer, 'very brilliant' is correct English.
Brilliant is already extreme, so we say absolutely brilliant, never very brilliant.
The man in Liverpool says the atmosphere at the stadium gives him goosebumps.
He told her it is so electric that it gives him goosebumps every time.

gapfill.text: This column runs on INTENSIFIERS. VERY, EXTREMELY + a normal adjective that can be stronger or weaker: 'VERY good', 'EXTREMELY loud'. ABSOLUTELY, UTTERLY, TOTALLY + an extreme adjective that is already at the top: 'ABSOLUTELY brilliant', 'UTTERLY flat'. REALLY works with both. SO + adjective, often with THAT: 'SO electric THAT it gives him goosebumps'. SUCH (A) + adjective + noun: 'SUCH A strange moment'.

bank.label: Useful language for talking about what you love
items: I have been hooked on it since I was a teenager.
It is absolutely brilliant, and here is why.
That song still gives me goosebumps.
The atmosphere was so electric that nobody sat down.
It was such a great night.
Sorry, I am getting carried away.
Old disco is my guilty pleasure.
I could geek out about this for hours.

lf.text: A and C, in blue, are extreme adjectives: brilliant and exhausted are already at the top, so they take ABSOLUTELY or TOTALLY. B and D are normal adjectives: good and loud can be stronger or weaker, so they take VERY or EXTREMELY. So ask yourself first: can this be a little bit true? If yes, use very. If no, use absolutely. And if you are not sure, really works with both.

items: Describe your favorite soul record to someone who has never heard it. Use one normal adjective with very or extremely, and one extreme adjective with absolutely.
Describe the most electric football match you have ever watched. Use so ... that and such a ...
A friend asks about your guilty pleasure. Tell them what it is, and say why you are a sucker for it.
A colleague says, 'Football is just a game.' Explain why it strikes a chord with millions of people, without getting carried away.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gap-fill: 1 = absolutely, 2 = very, 3 = utterly, 4 = such, 5 = so, 6 = totally.
Model (Scenario 1): 'The production is very simple, but the voice is absolutely incredible. The second verse still gives me goosebumps.'
Model (Scenario 2): 'It was such a tense final that I could not breathe. When we scored, the stadium was so loud that I lost my voice.'
Model (Scenario 3): 'Old disco is my guilty pleasure. I am a sucker for a big string section.'
Shapes: very / extremely + normal adjective. absolutely / utterly / totally + extreme adjective. really = both. so + adjective; such (a) + adjective + noun.
answerkey.note: Never use VERY with an extreme adjective: 'very amazing' and 'very exhausted' are wrong. Say 'absolutely amazing' or 'really exhausted'.

listenings.text: Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona. I listened to our interview again last night, and honestly, it was absolutely brilliant. My editor says your answer about soul music is the best part of the piece. She would like a photo of you with your records, if that is all right with you. One more thing. You told me that old disco is your guilty pleasure, and I laughed so much that I almost dropped my phone. Can I put that in the column too? If you say no, that is totally fine. Oh, and I am going to a match in Liverpool on Saturday. I am not a die-hard fan, but I hear the atmosphere is so electric that people lose their voices. Call me back when you can.

Welcome back to The Long Game. Today, a question from a listener in Brazil. He writes: when I talk about music in English, I sound like a weather report. Here is the problem, and it is extremely common. Most learners use one intensifier for everything: very. Very good, very nice, very interesting. Nothing is wrong with it, but it is utterly flat. So try this. First, keep very for normal adjectives, like good or tired. Second, when the feeling is bigger, change the adjective, not the volume. Do not say very good. Say brilliant, and if you mean it, absolutely brilliant. Third, give one detail. Passion is in the detail: the horn section in the second verse, the goal in the ninetieth minute. And finally, watch the person in front of you. If their eyes are glazing over, you are getting carried away. Enthusiasm is infectious, but only for about two minutes.

extra_audio.text: First, Fiona meets a friend in a tiny record shop in São Paulo, a die-hard fan who has been hooked on soul since he was fifteen. Then the friend describes the music in English as very good, and his words sound utterly flat. After that, Fiona explains that some adjectives, like good, take very, but extreme ones, like brilliant, take absolutely. Next, she watches a match in Liverpool with a fan whose stadium is so electric that it gives him goosebumps. Finally, she tells readers to say that what they love is absolutely amazing, and to tell people why.
